headline: Philly's underground runs on banned granite, North Philly stables and sparring gyms
summary: Philly's strongest scenes are street skating, hardcore, North Philly's Black horsemen, ballroom and boxing's "gym wars." The Sixers have an underground too: Process diehards, podcasters and bootleg-tee makers. They will judge the LeBron James and Jaylen Brown era faster than any campaign. Hardcore's sportswear crossover, North Philly Western wear and the new WNBA team are the open doors.

insights.title: LOVE Park made Philly an East Coast skate capital
insights.detail: From the early 1990s until the city's 2002 ban, LOVE Park's granite ledges made stars of Stevie Williams, Ricky Oyola and Josh Kalis. Williams went on to found DGK. Planner Ed Bacon skated the park at 92 in protest, and the city turned down DC Shoes' $1 million offer to keep it open. The scene moved to Paine's Park on the Schuylkill (2013) and the DIY concrete of FDR Skatepark under I-95. Its look is DGK's oversized, hip-hop cut, not California thrash.
insights.implication: Skate is Nike's most credible door here. Go through Nike SB, with skaters from the LOVE and Paine's lineage, and put real money into Franklin's Paine Skatepark Fund. Cut Sixers product for skaters big and hip-hop, not Portland workwear.

insights.title: Philly hardcore already moshes in basketball gear
insights.detail: This Is Hardcore, the summer festival held in Philadelphia since the mid-2000s, anchors the scene. Bands like Soul Glo, Jesus Piece and Mannequin Pussy make the city a national hardcore and punk hub. Crowds two-step in mesh shorts, oversized jerseys over thermals and running shoes. Bands sell custom jerseys as merch.
insights.implication: This crowd ignores team-store product but already wears the silhouette. A boxier Sixers "show jersey," made with a Philly band (licensed and paid), reaches a style-leading audience that mainstream hoops marketing misses.

insights.title: Fletcher Street's Black cowboys had the Western look first
insights.detail: Black horsemen have kept stables around Fletcher Street in North Philadelphia for generations. The Fletcher Street Urban Riding Club teaches neighborhood kids to ride and care for horses. Netflix's Concrete Cowboy (2021, with Idris Elba) put real riders on screen. They ride in hoodies, fitted caps and work boots with saddle leather, a mix that predates the 2024 Western-wear wave.
insights.implication: This is the market's most original style story, and it belongs to the riders. Design any capsule with the club, cast its riders instead of models, and fund the stables, which have fought for years to secure a permanent home.

insights.title: Philly made the Pride flag Black and brown
insights.detail: In June 2017, after a 2016 reckoning over racism in Gayborhood bars, the city's Office of LGBT Affairs added black and brown stripes to the rainbow flag. The design now flies worldwide. Philly Black Pride anchors a ballroom scene of Black and Latino houses. Landmarks include Giovanni's Room, the oldest LGBTQ bookstore in the U.S. (founded 1973, now run by Philly AIDS Thrift), and Bob & Barbara's long-running drag night.
insights.implication: Philly gives Nike's Be True program a real origin story, but only if Black and brown LGBTQ Philadelphians co-create the product. Time it to Black Pride in spring as well as June, and pay and credit the ballroom talent.

insights.title: "Gym wars" beat the Rocky steps
insights.detail: Philadelphia boxing is known for "gym wars," sparring fought at full intensity. The culture runs from Joe Frazier's North Broad gym (closed, but on the National Register) through Front Street Gym to today's Jaron "Boots" Ennis. Club cards at the 2300 Arena, the former ECW Arena where 1990s hardcore wrestling was born, keep the fight-night scene alive.
insights.implication: "Gym wars" is a ready story for Sixers training gear in a season of maximum pressure on Nick Nurse and an aging core. Think heavyweight fleece, reinforced seams and a working gym's co-sign. Nike owns Philly toughness without licensing Rocky.

insights.title: The Sixers' own underground wrote "Trust the Process"
insights.detail: During Sam Hinkie's 2013-16 rebuild, Sixers Twitter, the Liberty Ballers blog and The Rights to Ricky Sanchez podcast turned "Trust the Process" into a creed. That was before Joel Embiid took it as a nickname. Fans printed their own shirts ("Hinkie Died for Your Sins"). The LeBron James and Jaylen Brown era brings a 41-year-old star and a former Celtic. It will test that crowd's loyalty and irony, and bootleg tees will answer every win and loss within hours.
insights.implication: Win this crowd with speed and self-awareness. Make quick-turn, one-color tees co-signed with fan creators, and product that honors the Process lineage around Embiid. A polished LeBron-first launch is one they will mock.

insights.title: Sons of Ben is the template for Philly's WNBA team
insights.detail: Soccer fans founded the Sons of Ben in 2007, before the Union existed, and helped win the MLS franchise. They still lead the River End at Subaru Park in Chester with tifo, scarves and chants. Philadelphia's WNBA team, due in 2030 in the new South Philly arena, has no supporters' culture yet.
insights.implication: As the WNBA's uniform partner, Nike can help a founding supporters' group form now, with scarves, tifo kits and pre-launch "founder" gear. Borrow the Sons of Ben model. Union kits are Adidas, so copy the playbook, not the club.

places.name: Paine's Park
places.neighborhood: Fairmount (Schuylkill riverfront below the Art Museum)
places.why: The plaza-style park Philly skaters won after the LOVE Park ban, and the natural stage for any Nike SB x Sixers launch.

places.name: FDR Skatepark
places.why: Skater-built concrete under the interstate since 1994. One of the world's most famous DIY parks, a few minutes from the arena.

places.name: Fletcher Street Urban Riding Club
places.why: Home of Philly's Black urban horsemen and the real story behind Concrete Cowboy.

places.name: Front Street Gym
places.why: One of the gyms where "gym wars" sparring earned Philly its reputation for hard fighters.

places.name: 2300 Arena
places.neighborhood: South Philadelphia (Swanson Street, by the sports complex)
places.why: The former ECW Arena, birthplace of 1990s hardcore wrestling, still runs club boxing and indie wrestling cards.

places.name: Philly AIDS Thrift @ Giovanni's Room
places.why: The oldest LGBTQ bookstore in the U.S. (1973) is now a thrift-and-books shop whose sales fund HIV/AIDS groups. A vintage stop for the queer scene.

places.name: Bob & Barbara's Lounge
places.why: Birthplace of the "Citywide Special" and home to one of the city's longest-running weekly drag shows.

places.name: William Way LGBT Community Center
places.why: Home of Philly's LGBTQ archive and community, and a natural partner and beneficiary for any Pride product.

places.name: Underground Arts
places.why: A basement venue under the Wolf Building that hosts much of the city's hardcore, punk and late-night dance programming.

places.name: Atmos USA (former Ubiq site), Walnut Street
places.why: Philly's best-known independent sneaker boutique and the most credible store to seed a limited Sixers footwear drop.

people.name: Ricky Oyola
people.why: Philly-born pioneer of raw East Coast street skating. His 1990s LOVE Park and Center City footage still defines the city's skate identity.

people.name: Franklin's Paine Skatepark Fund
people.why: The skater-led group that got Paine's Park built, and the right channel for Nike SB money and permissions.

people.name: Soul Glo
people.why: A Black-led Philly hardcore band (on Epitaph) whose sound and politics put the city's scene in the national conversation.

people.name: Mannequin Pussy
people.why: Another Philly punk band on Epitaph, with a large queer and young-women following that crosses the DIY and indie scenes.

people.name: Jaron 'Boots' Ennis
people.why: Philadelphia's current boxing star, trained by his father in the city's gym tradition, and the face of "gym wars" for a new generation.

people.name: The Rights to Ricky Sanchez
people.role: Sixers fan podcast (Michael Levin and Spike Eskin)
people.why: The Process era's defining fan media. It helped turn "Trust the Process" into a movement and still speaks for the diehards.

people.name: Sons of Ben
people.why: The region's model supporters' culture, built before its club existed. It is the template for Philadelphia's WNBA fan base.

people.name: Philly Black Pride
people.role: Black LGBTQ organization and annual Pride weekend
people.why: The center of Philly's Black queer and ballroom community, and the right partner for any Pride capsule.

moments.name: Union home matches with the Sons of Ben
moments.timing: Late February to October, Subaru Park, Chester
moments.why: Tailgates, tifo, scarves and the River End: a live look at the supporters' culture Philadelphia's WNBA team will need.

moments.name: Philly Black Pride
moments.why: The anchor weekend for Black LGBTQ Philadelphians and the ballroom scene, and a better launch window for co-created Pride product than crowded June.

moments.name: Kensington Kinetic Sculpture Derby and Trenton Avenue Arts Festival
moments.why: East Kensington's DIY maker day. Homemade human-powered sculptures race through a mud pit, and printmakers press giant woodblocks with a steamroller.

moments.name: PHL Pride March and Festival
moments.why: The citywide Pride in the Gayborhood, reorganized by a community collective after 2021. The eight-stripe flag flies on home turf.

moments.name: This Is Hardcore
moments.why: The national hardcore scene's summer gathering in Philadelphia, and the best place to see how the scene wears jerseys and mesh shorts.

moments.name: Fight nights at the 2300 Arena
moments.timing: Club boxing and indie wrestling cards through the year
moments.why: Where Philly's fight and wrestling diehards gather, and where local boxers build followings before the big arenas.

vocabulary.meaning: Skaters' name for JFK Plaza (LOVE Park). "Skating LOVE" means the golden era from the early 1990s to the 2002 ban.
Philly boxing slang for sparring fought at full intensity, like a real bout. Surviving them is a badge of the city's gyms.
A cheap beer-and-a-shot combo. The "Citywide Special" started at Bob & Barbara's on South Street and spread to bars across the city.
The Hinkie-era rebuilding creed that fans turned into an identity, and Joel Embiid into a nickname. Saying "Trust the Process" now is loyalty, irony or both.
Philly address term for a Muslim man, from the Arabic "akhi" (my brother), now used more broadly. It reflects the city's deep Black Muslim roots, so it is not a print gimmick.
The Union supporters' end at Subaru Park, led by the Sons of Ben, where the region's tifo and chant culture lives.

designCues.cue: LOVE-ledge granite: charcoal-gray speckled stone (base about #5E5D5A with pale #A8A49C flecks) with worn, waxed edges.
designCues.source: The granite ledges and steps of LOVE Park, skated from the early 1990s until the 2002 ban and the plaza's later rebuild.
designCues.use: Use it as a jacquard or printed speckle on fleece, skate-durable shorts and shoe uppers. Never use Robert Indiana's LOVE letters, which are licensed IP.

designCues.cue: More Color More Pride brown (#784F17), paired with black, as the two stripes above the rainbow.
designCues.source: Philadelphia's 2017 eight-stripe Pride flag, added by the city's Office of LGBT Affairs after a reckoning over racism in Gayborhood bars.
designCues.use: Use it only in a Pride capsule co-created with Black and brown LGBTQ Philadelphians. Try a brown-and-black stripe on the jock tag or waistband, with the origin story on the hangtag.

designCues.cue: Show-jersey layering: an oversized, longer mesh jersey over a waffle thermal, below-the-knee mesh shorts and crew socks pulled high.
designCues.source: This Is Hardcore and Philly club and basement shows, where crowds two-step in basketball gear and bands sell custom jerseys.
designCues.use: Sell a boxier, longer Sixers mesh jersey and thermal underlayer as a set. License any band graphic and pay the band.

designCues.cue: Saddle leather and stable workwear: tan tooled leather (about #8B5A2B), saddle stitching, rope piping and duck canvas.
designCues.source: The Fletcher Street stables, where riders mix Western tack with hoodies, fitted caps and work boots.
designCues.use: Put leather trim and saddle-stitch details on a varsity or coaches jacket built with the club and credited by name, with proceeds to its stables. No costume cowboy hats or bandanas.

designCues.cue: Steamroller relief print: oversize carved-woodblock graphics pressed by a road roller, with uneven ink, visible wood grain and block edges.
designCues.source: The Kensington Kinetic Sculpture Derby and Trenton Avenue Arts Festival, where printmakers press giant blocks with a steamroller.
designCues.use: Use it for hand-pressed graphic tees or a jersey-number print pulled from blocks carved by Kensington printmakers, so each piece is slightly different.

designCues.cue: Gym wars: the sparring gym as Philly's proving ground.
designCues.source: Philadelphia boxing's full-intensity sparring culture, from Joe Frazier's North Broad gym to Front Street Gym and Jaron "Boots" Ennis.
designCues.use: Make it the story for a Sixers training collection (heavyweight fleece, reinforced seams, sparring-cut shorts). Shoot it in a working gym, pay its fighters, and skip licensing Rocky.

designCues.cue: Process-era bootleg graphics: blunt sans-serif slogans, low-res fan photos and saint-style halo iconography, screen-printed in one or two colors on cheap tees.
designCues.source: Fan-made shirts sold online and outside the arena during the 2013-18 rebuild.
designCues.use: Use it for quick-turn, one-color slogan tees co-signed by fan creators. Keep Sam Hinkie's likeness and "Trust the Process" off product unless the rights are cleared.

productHooks: "LOVE Ledge" Nike SB x Sixers capsule: granite-speckle fleece, baggy skate shorts and a Sixers-colorway SB Dunk, designed with skaters from the LOVE and Paine's lineage. Launch at Paine's Park with a donation to Franklin's Paine Skatepark Fund, and no LOVE sculpture letters.
"Show Jersey" set: a boxier, longer Sixers mesh jersey sold with a waffle thermal and one licensed graphic by a Philly hardcore or punk band. Release it the week of This Is Hardcore in late July.

Fletcher Street capsule: a saddle-stitched, leather-trimmed varsity jacket and stable-canvas work pants, co-designed with the Fletcher Street Urban Riding Club and modeled by its riders. A fixed share of proceeds goes to a permanent stables fund.

Philly Be True drop for Philly Black Pride in late April: brown-and-black stripe details (#784F17) on Sixers warm-ups and a ballroom-ready cropped mesh jersey. Co-design with Philly Black Pride and local houses, and send proceeds to William Way or a group they choose.

"Founders" supporters kit for Philadelphia's WNBA team: scarves, tifo-painting kits and pre-name "founding member" tees, seeded with a fan collective years before the 2030 tip-off. Follow the Sons of Ben model.
"Gym Wars" training line: heavyweight fleece and sparring-cut shorts, shot at Front Street Gym with Philly fighters and released into the spring playoff push.
watchouts: Dirt bikes, ATVs and street takeovers are Philly's loudest street scenes. They are also illegal on city streets, linked to fatal crashes and targeted by police seizures. Never stage, sponsor or depict them, however strong the imagery. Stay out of car culture, gaming, anime and street dance too: they are less distinctive here than elsewhere.

Kensington Avenue under the El is the center of the city's opioid crisis, so no "gritty" shoots or graphics there. East Kensington's and Fishtown's DIY scenes are also tense about gentrification. Work through established neighborhood groups.

The eight-stripe flag came out of a fight over racism in the Gayborhood, and Black and Latino trans and queer people lead ballroom. Using either without co-creators, credit and pay will be called out fast. The beards and kufis of the city's large Black Muslim community are religious practice, not a style cue.

Licensing and likeness: all of these need clearance. That means Robert Indiana's LOVE, Rocky, Concrete Cowboy (Netflix), band names, the This Is Hardcore name and Sam Hinkie's likeness. It also means "Trust the Process," which Embiid has sought to trademark.

Brand conflicts run through these scenes. Stevie Williams built DGK, Allen Iverson is Reebok, Embiid moved to Skechers and Jaylen Brown is building his own 741 line. LeBron James is Nike's anchor on this roster. Confirm Maxey's and Edgecombe's footwear deals before outreach.
